summary: A 1970 note recording conversations with Steve Crocker at UCLA. It is informal documentation of discussion about network proposals, not a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 49 records discussions about the proposed NCP in RFC 46. It reports agreement on keeping data unstructured at the NCP level and describes debate about interrupts, socket identifiers, and a standard login protocol.

questions: what did crocker and meyer discuss
should the ncp impose data structure
subtitle: A record of discussions about NCP and user login protocol choices.

tldr.problem: The NCP proposal raised unresolved questions about interrupts, socket identifiers, data handling, queueing, and how users should log in to remote hosts.
tldr.mechanism: Edwin Meyer records telephone discussions with Steve Crocker and Tom Skinner, distinguishing areas of agreement from open questions and disagreements.
tldr.outcome: RFC 49 is an informal discussion note about RFC 46, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 49 is an informal historical record of discussions about the proposal in RFC 46. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Interrupts, Identifiers, and Data
sections.content:
Meyer reports that Crocker supported an INT command for reliably interrupting a process that agreed to accept interrupts over a socket connection. The NCP would not define the interrupt handler; a higher-level protocol would do that.

The participants did not settle whether socket identifiers should include an instance tag. They agreed that the NCP should not impose a special structure on transmitted data, which they treated as bit strings of arbitrary length, and that optional echoing should not be part of the NCP protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The discussion supports an interrupt command but leaves its meaning to higher-level protocols. It favors leaving data format decisions above NCP and leaves socket instance tags unresolved.

sections.title: Queueing and Connection Requests
sections.content:
Meyer's proposal would queue connection requests only for open sockets and reject requests to inactive or connected sockets. Crocker suggests briefly queueing requests for sockets in an unacceptable state, then rejecting them after a specified interval.

Meyer says this limited queueing could support protocol interactions involving timing races and does not seem unreasonable to him.
sections.plainLanguage: The participants consider whether a connection request should be rejected at once or held briefly while a socket is unavailable. Meyer finds a short wait reasonable.

sections.title: The User Control and Communication Protocol
sections.content:
The participants discuss a User Control and Communication (UCC) protocol for creating a user process at a foreign host. Crocker objects to Meyer's approach because it requires two full-duplex connections and switching between them; he proposes using sockets 0 and 1 for requests to a logger.

Meyer lists possible security and access problems with that approach, including a process using another user's socket code. He argues that a standard UCC protocol should be implemented at all sites so users can communicate across hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The note compares ways to handle remote login and describes concerns about tying up or misusing socket identifiers. Meyer argues for one UCC protocol shared across sites.

references.text: Meyer, E. E., "ARPA Network Protocol Notes", NWG/RFC 46, 1970.
